leading_positions.synthesis: All six round 1 files name Mircea Cărtărescu as the single preferred laureate, so only one candidate is explicitly preferred. The shared grounds are distinctiveness of voice, formal ambition at large scale, and an imaginative project that appears to extend across volumes and genres. Each member also states that the identical first places are not evidence of merit and that the claim needs testing. What is not shared is the citation scope. Mattson and Olsson frame it around prose or the novel's means. Carlberg, Palm and Sward include poetry (Palm as 'poetry as its ground'). Sem-Sandberg and Sward place the work in a 'European tradition of inward and fantastic narrative'. The members also differ on how heavily the translation, length and unevenness reservations should weigh. Every member rests the judgment on public knowledge and translation reception, not on independent reading of the Romanian originals. Named alternatives differ by member: Carson (B027) appears in five alternative lists (Carlberg, Olsson, Palm, Sem-Sandberg, Sward) and is ranked sixth by Mattson. Yan Lianke (B002) appears in three (Carlberg, Mattson, Sward). Adonis (B035) appears in two (Olsson, Sem-Sandberg). Murnane (B001) appears in one (Mattson), and Wright (B029) in one (Palm). Alternatives are not counted as preferences.

areas_of_agreement: All six members explicitly prefer one single-writer configuration, B024 (Mircea Cărtărescu), with no multiwriter or no-award position stated in round 1.
All six members state that the coinciding first-place rankings are not evidence of literary merit and that the case should be tested against the texts and the common criteria.

All six members record the same main limitation: the Cărtărescu case depends on Romanian prose texture, rhythm and long-sentence control that translation may flatten, and their judgments rest on public knowledge and reception, not independent reading.
Members agree that coverage of Cărtărescu's poetry, early work and essays in translation is thinner than for the major novels, so the corpus is covered unevenly.

Members agree that the case should rest on literary form and language, not on nationality, political symbolism, censorship, publication circumstances, age or timing. This is stated explicitly for Yan Lianke, Wright and Adonis.
Members agree that Adonis's essays and public positions should be kept apart from the judgment of his poetry, and that Arabic prosody is the part of his achievement that translation loses most.
Members agree that Wright's compact corpus of major novels makes sustained quality harder to establish, although Palm argues that scale and formal reinvention can still carry the case.
Members agree that the reach of Carson's oeuvre depends on settling which strands (original verse and essay, hybrid book-objects, classical translations and scholarship) count as the core.
scientific_disputes: Whether Cărtărescu's maximalist, self-referential long novels sustain quality across their full length or are uneven or excessive. Members state this concern but none can verify it. Olsson and Carlberg read the public record as showing development, while Mattson, Sward and Sem-Sandberg leave it open.

Whether his breadth of significance extends beyond readers of ambitious fiction. Palm answers that breadth lies in joining the intimate to the encyclopedic and in reach across poetry and prose, while Mattson and Sward treat this as unresolved.

Whether Carson's genre hybridity is a core literary achievement or a series of brilliant experiments. Palm suggests it may be a developing method. Mattson, Carlberg and Olsson ask for it to be shown across volumes.
Whether Murnane's deliberately narrow range is a strength (intensity and consistency, Mattson) or a limit on significance across a body of work (Carlberg, Olsson, Palm, Sem-Sandberg, Sward).

How Yan Lianke's mythorealist grotesque should be judged. Sward argues from narrative form and sustained imaginative force across decades. Sem-Sandberg, Mattson, Carlberg and Olsson cite uneven translation quality, restricted circulation and uncertain consistency across many titles.

How the will's reference to an idealistic tendency applies to an inward, encyclopedic and often disturbing project (Olsson), or to formally radical and ironic work such as Carson's (Carlberg, Palm, Sward). Members call it a matter of interpretation. Olsson and Sward decline to treat it as settled or as grounds for exclusion without a shared reading.
How to weigh singularity and scale of a single project against breadth when comparing differently shaped oeuvres (Palm).
attribution_disputes: Every file credits one writer, Mircea Cărtărescu, so no dispute over laureate identity or sharing arises. The differences concern citation scope only.

The proposed citations differ on genre. Mattson's and Olsson's wording centers prose or the novel. Carlberg's and Sward's name prose and poetry, and Palm's frames fiction as the core with poetry as its ground.

The citations differ on framing: 'renewing the novel's means' (Carlberg, Mattson, Olsson), 'cosmological imaginative world' (Palm), and 'the European tradition of inward and fantastic narrative' (Sem-Sandberg, Sward). Sem-Sandberg and Sward say national symbolism should not shape the wording.

For Carson, attribution turns on whether classical translations and scholarship are context or part of the citation scope. Carlberg would treat them as context, Sem-Sandberg would make the original poetry and verse narrative the core, and Palm notes they sit at the edge of the creative oeuvre.
For Adonis, members would confine the case to the poems and to critical prose about poetic language. For Wright, Olsson and Sward raise whether nonfiction and recent work belong in the scope.
maturity_disputes: For Cărtărescu, members ask whether the later very long novels deepen the early project or repeat it, and whether sustained quality is spread across the oeuvre or concentrated in a few peaks (Carlberg's stated test).
For Carson, members ask whether sustained quality across many volumes can be shown, or whether weight rests on Autobiography of Red and Nox (Carlberg, Mattson, Olsson, Sem-Sandberg, Sward).
For Wright, members ask whether the later and nonfiction work deepen Carpentaria and The Swan Book or only extend them. Palm acknowledges the size of the oeuvre.
For Michon, Mattson and Sem-Sandberg treat a slim corpus as a limit on breadth, while Mattson values the exceptional sentences.
For Adonis, Sward asks whether sustained quality in recent decades can be judged, since his main formal influence may belong to earlier decades.
For Yan Lianke, Carlberg, Mattson and Sem-Sandberg ask how quality holds across a large body of titles given uneven translation.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: No member reports a connection to any shortlisted writer or requests recusal in the round 1 files.
Carlberg is a co-opted member whose actual committee voting status is undocumented, so her simulated vote is a modeling assumption.

Members mention their own practice or scholarly interests (the chair's modern poetry and exile literature, novelistic practice, Palm's myth and ekphrasis, Sem-Sandberg's Central Europe work). All are stated as context, not as evidence of preference. These are disclosed and not adjudicated.
questions_for_round2: For Cărtărescu, which specific later volumes, and which strands of the poetry, shorter prose and essays, best show that the late work deepens the early project and not merely extends it? What would count against that claim?

Should the citation name prose only, or prose and poetry? Should the framing be 'renewing the novel's means', 'a cosmological imaginative world', or 'the European tradition of inward and fantastic narrative'? What wording avoids national symbolism?

How should the committee weigh reliance on translation for Romanian long-sentence control? What forms of evidence (translators' accounts, Romanian-language expert assessments, reception) would members accept as adequate, and are Arabic- or Chinese-reading assessments needed for Adonis and Yan Lianke?

For Carson, can members agree on the core oeuvre (original poetry, verse narrative and essays, with translations and scholarship as context)? If so, does sustained quality across volumes hold up better than the concentration in Autobiography of Red and Nox that several members suspect?
Is Murnane's narrow range a limit on significance across a body of work, or a legitimate form of intensity? What standard of breadth should apply equally to Murnane, Michon and Wright?

How should the committee read the will's reference to an idealistic tendency for an inward, encyclopedic and often disturbing project (Cărtărescu) and for ironic, formally radical work (Carson)? Is there a shared reading before it is applied to any candidate?
Do Wright's later and nonfiction works, and Yan Lianke's wider titles, change the sustained-quality assessment enough for either to be tested head to head against B024?
summary.chair_observation: Round 1 shows explicit support from all six members for a single laureate, B024 (Mircea Cărtărescu), and no explicit support for any other configuration or for no award. The files give consistent reasons and consistent reservations. The remaining uncertainty is evidential: the translation dependence of the prose case, unverified unevenness in the late long novels, and the unresolved questions of citation scope and the will's idealistic tendency. The alternatives (Carson, Yan Lianke, Adonis, Murnane, Wright) differ by member and are not preferences. Because no member has independent reading of the originals, round 2 should test the claims against the specific evidence members can cite, without treating the agreement on first place as evidence of merit.
